rv.q: Appealing as Boseman's writing is, the play feels padded in places

It’s so ambitious and overfull that we lose sight of the main trail in places: it could do with trimming back and when it goes full-on revenge saga at the end it becomes rather melodramatic and heavy-handed.
This is an ambitious, unfocused work by a young writer exploring the reach of his talent.
The play is packed with ideas, and there is a surrendering pleasure in submitting to its strange logic and poetic richness.
Boseman’s bleakly poetic but playful exploration of grief is devastating at its best but I found the first half a bit of a chore.
It’s an incredibly thoughtful, beautifully acted production, that creates its own atmosphere.
As it is, we’re left lamenting the ongoing pertinence of a play steeped in anger at the “price of a Black man’s life” here performed with a revivifying passion.
It is flawed, brilliant, busy, overwritten, charged with restless creative energy and bracing imagination.

Instead, this production of Deep Azure does immense honour to a script that feels more at home in Shakespeare’s Globe than anything else written since the bard’s death.

Although nearly three hours is decidedly long for something that I often could not properly understand and from the upper gallery with candelabra usually closer to me than faces, making it often difficult to see, I still enjoyed it.
As it is, the negative aspects of the project drag the positives down irreparably.

cn.t: Boseman's ambitious verse play blending hip-hop and Shakespeare earns praise for its lyrical power and timely themes of police brutality, though some critics find it overstuffed and overlong. A poignant showcase of the late actor's lost writing talent.
